extracted.intended_audience: public speakers, humorists, and fund-raisers (general audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and embedded principles for delivering humorous speeches, entertaining addresses, and fundraising remarks—drawn from Mark Twain's examples and asides about rhetoric, storytelling, audience management, and interview tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a story to deliver the moral
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is this advantage about a story... whatever moral or valuable thing you put into a speech, why, it gets diffused among those involuted sentences and possibly your audience goes away without finding out what that valuable thing was... you put the same jewel into a story and it becomes the keystone of that story — you are bound to get it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer embedding your lesson or thesis inside a concrete, entertaining anecdote rather than stating it didactically. Twain demonstrates this by turning a moral (the ‘lost opportunity’) into a narrated incident that ensures the audience perceives the point — the story makes the moral obvious and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: When you lack substantive material, 'play a part' (adopt a persona)
rubrics_metrics.description: “When I am situated like that, with nothing to say, I feel as though I were a sort of fraud; I seem to be playing a part, and please consider I am playing a part... I have often done this before.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you arrive without a firm text or original content, intentionally adopt a stage persona or comic role to carry the occasion. Acting a character (self-deprecating, whimsical, befuddled, etc.) can cover thin content while entertaining the audience; consistency and naturalness in the persona are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: French-speech convention (parody): cite dates, not events
rubrics_metrics.description: “A French sermon is like a French speech — it never names an historical event, but only the date of it; if you are not up in dates, you get left.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain's parody identifies an identifiable rhetorical habit: speeches that rely on lists of dates and formal allusions rather than narrative explanation. If imitating or critiquing that style, emphasize enumerated dates and grandiloquent references; if attending such a speech, be prepared with historical-date knowledge or expect to miss the references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundraising/fair etiquette: do not coerce purchases; charity should not be exploitative
rubrics_metrics.description: “At this fair no one is to be persecuted to buy. If you offer a twenty-dollar bill in payment for a purchase of $1 you will receive $19 in change. There is to be no robbery here. There is to be no creed here—no religion except charity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When managing a charitable event or market, avoid hard-sell or coercive tactics; be scrupulous and honest about transactions (give correct change), and frame the occasion around voluntary giving and humane purpose rather than pressure or sectarian appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview tactic: give contradictory facts to flummox the interviewer; remain charming
rubrics_metrics.description: “Whenever you give the interviewer a fact, give him another fact that will contradict it. Then he'll go away with a jumble that he can't use at all. Be gentle, be sweet, smile like an idiot—just be natural.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn interviews (or intrusive questioning) into a controlled performance: supply colorful, conflicting details so the interviewer cannot produce a coherent, usable account. Do this while maintaining a friendly, disarming demeanor — it’s a technique of evasive humor and narrative control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open with compliments and audience flattery to warm the room
rubrics_metrics.description: “I have no text except what you furnish me with your handsome faces... compliments should be in order in a place like this.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by flattering the audience (appearance, generosity, local pride) to establish goodwill and signal congenial intent. Compliments can buy patience and create a receptive atmosphere for anecdote and appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use self-deprecation and comic exaggeration as devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples throughout (e.g., ‘Perhaps I am not a humorist, but I am a first-class fool—a simpleton;’ contradictory biographical claims to an interviewer) show Twain placing himself as the comic butt or absurd figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positioning oneself as fallible, foolish, or exaggeratedly boastful invites laughter and disarms criticism. Combine self-mockery with absurd specificities (contradictory birthplace, impossible ages) to generate comic effect and deflect seriousness.
